questions.question: What makes reverse syllogism different from classic syllogism?
options: The conclusions are given first and you pick the statement set that makes them true
The statements are always negative
You must evaluate real-world truth of each option
Only three options are given instead of four
questions.rationale: In reverse syllogism the conclusions are given and four option sets of statements are provided; you pick the set from which those conclusions definitely follow. The input and output of the classic form are swapped.

questions.question: What is the first step of the reverse-syllogism method taught in this lesson?
options: Draw the Venn pictures demanded by each conclusion before looking at any option
Convert every statement in every option
Eliminate options that contain universal statements
Check which option sounds true in the real world
questions.rationale: The method is conclusions first: translate each conclusion into a Venn requirement and a kill list, then scan the options against it. Construction of statement sets is rarely needed.

questions.question: Conclusions: Some cars are buses. No bus is a cycle. Which option set supports both conclusions?
options: All cars are buses. All buses are cycles.
Some cars are buses. No bus is a cycle.
All cars are cycles. Some cycles are buses.
No car is a bus. No bus is a cycle.
questions.rationale: Option (b) states both conclusions outright, so both are definitely true. Option (a) kills conclusion II, option (c) kills it too, and option (d) contradicts conclusion I.

questions.question: Why does 'All cars are cycles. Some cycles are buses.' fail the conclusion 'No bus is a cycle'?
options: Because cycles are never mentioned
Because some cycles being buses means at least one bus is a cycle
Because all cars are cycles
Because the option has no negative statement
questions.rationale: Some cycles are buses guarantees an overlap between the bus and cycle circles, directly contradicting 'No bus is a cycle'. The kill list catches this in seconds.

questions.question: What does the statement 'Only a few A are B' mean?
options: Some A are B, and possibly all A are B
Some A are B AND some A are not B
No A is a B
All A are B
questions.rationale: Only a few A are B carries two commitments: at least one A is a B, and at least one A is not a B. It is strictly stronger than plain 'some'.

questions.question: Statement: Only a few doctors are surgeons. Which conclusion is definitely FALSE?
options: Some doctors are surgeons
Some doctors are not surgeons
All doctors are surgeons
Some surgeons being doctors is a possibility
questions.rationale: Only a few doctors are surgeons guarantees some doctors are outside the surgeon circle, so 'All doctors are surgeons' is contradicted and definitely false. The two 'some' conclusions are definitely true.

questions.question: How should the phrase 'A can never be B' be treated?
options: As a possibility claim needing one supporting arrangement
As equivalent to 'No A is B', demanding definite proof of total separation
As a statement about real-world facts
As identical to 'only a few A are B'
questions.rationale: 'Can never be' is the mirror of possibility: it translates to 'No A is B' and demands the strongest proof. A single arrangement where an A sits inside B destroys it.

questions.question: Statements: Only a few pens are pencils. No pencil is a marker. Does 'Pens can never be markers' follow?
options: Yes, because no pencil is a marker
No, because the statements never separate pens from markers
Yes, because only a few pens are pencils
No, because only a few means some are
questions.rationale: Nothing in the statements separates the pen and marker circles — they are never mentioned together — so 'No pen is a marker' is not definitely true and the conclusion does not follow.

questions.question: Which type of statement eliminates reverse-syllogism options fastest?
options: The E-type ('No X is Y')
The I-type ('Some X are Y')
Any statement about the conclusion's predicate
The longest statement in the option
questions.rationale: A single No-statement contradicts the largest number of possible conclusions, so it should sit at the top of your kill list and eliminate options fastest.

questions.question: According to the lesson's timing advice, what should you do if two options are still alive after two minutes?
options: Guess immediately and move on
Look for the E-type or 'only a few' statement to break the tie
Rebuild all four diagrams from scratch
Choose the option with more statements
questions.rationale: The budget is about two minutes per question; if two options survive, hunt for the E-type or only-a-few statement — one of them almost always breaks the tie. If still stuck, mark and skip.
